title: Bēowulf
titleEn: Beowulf — Fitt XXVI: Farewell to Heorot (lines 1817–1887)
source: Fr. Klaeber, Beowulf and the Fight at Finnsburg, 1st edition (Boston: D. C. Heath & Co., 1922), pp. 68–70, lines 1817–1887 (fitt XXVI). Text follows Klaeber's printing exactly — þ, ð, æ, vowel-length macrons, a circumflex for contracted vowels (Klaeber prints one mark over the pair of vowels; we place it on the second), [brackets] for letters or words added by emendation, (parentheses) for conjectural restoration of fire-damaged letters, and Klaeber's rows of dots where words are lost. A dot under a vowel (dōgọra) is Klaeber's sign that the vowel does not count in the metre. Transcribed from the page images of the archive.org scan, every page read twice. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed late West Saxon, c. 1000, following Campbell's Old English Grammar — and the recorded reading follows it, within stated limits. No synthetic voice for Old English exists, so the reading is produced by an American English neural voice under per-word phonetic pinning: every sound is specified outright rather than left to modern English habits. So æ is the vowel of 'cat' and a the open back vowel of 'father'; short and long vowels stay apart; ea and eo are sounded as two-part diphthongs; sc is 'sh', cg the 'j' of 'edge', hw a breathy w; h after a vowel is the rasp of German 'ach' or 'ich'; and doubled consonants are held long. The limits: the voice has no throaty g (dagas, lagu), so it says a plain g; long ǣ, long ȳ and long ēa are heard short; compounds are not split, so a sound at the seam of a compound is occasionally voiced where it should not be; and unstressed vowels keep their full quality. The reading is a model of one scholarly convention, as much a reconstruction as the text. Translations made fresh from the original.
about: Beowulf survives in a single manuscript, the Nowell Codex, which was scorched in a library fire in 1731; its edges have crumbled away, and some readings survive only in two transcripts made in 1787. What you read here is a reconstruction — Klaeber's edition of 1922 — and parts of it are educated guesswork: [brackets] mark letters editors added, (parentheses) mark letters restored where the manuscript is damaged or lost, and a few words are best guesses whose exact meaning no one knows. The notes say so where it matters. Line numbers are Klaeber's, the standard way of citing the poem.

sentences.t: Bēowulf maþelode, bearn Ecgþēowes:
sentences.l: Beowulf spoke in speech-words, child of Ecgtheow:
sentences.i: Beowulf spoke in formal words, the son of Ecgtheow:
sentences.n: The house rendering of the speech formula, as at 1651: ‘maþelode’ is the past of ‘maþelian’, the verb that opens a formal speech, and ‘bearn Ecgþēowes’ is ‘child of Ecgtheow’, ‘bearn’ nominative in apposition to the name and ‘Ecgþēowes’ genitive. The colon opens Beowulf’s leave-taking.

sentences.t:
‘Nū wē sǣlīðend secgan wyllað
feorran cumene, þæt wē fundiaþ
Higelāc sēcan.
sentences.l: ‘Now we sea-farers, come from afar, wish to say that we are bent on seeking Higelac.
sentences.i: ‘Now we seafarers, who have come from far away, wish to say that we are eager to go and find Higelac.
sentences.n: ‘wē sǣlīðend … feorran cumene’ is ‘we sea-farers come from afar’: ‘sǣlīðend’ is a nominative plural (‘sǣ’ ‘sea’ and ‘līðend’ ‘traveller’, from ‘līðan’, ‘sail’), and ‘cumene’ is the plural past participle of ‘cuman’, agreeing with ‘wē’. ‘secgan wyllað’ is ‘wish to say’, ‘wyllað’ being the plural of ‘willan’, ‘will, wish’, with an infinitive, and the ‘þæt’ clause gives what they say: ‘þæt wē fundiaþ Higelāc sēcan’, ‘that we are bent on seeking Higelac’, ‘fundiaþ’ being the plural of ‘fundian’, ‘strive, hasten’, with ‘sēcan’ an infinitive and ‘Higelāc’ its accusative object. The opening quotation mark is Klaeber’s, as printed in ‘t’. Higelac is Beowulf’s lord and uncle.

sentences.t:
Wǣron hēr tela,
willum bewenede;
sentences.l: We were here well, supplied with wishes;
sentences.i: We have been well treated here, supplied as we wished;
sentences.n: ‘Wǣron’ is the plural past of ‘wesan’, ‘were’, and the subject is the Geats, carried over from ‘wē’ in the last unit. ‘hēr’ is ‘here’ and ‘tela’ ‘well’. ‘willum bewenede’ is ‘provided with wishes’: ‘bewenede’ is a plural past participle of ‘bewenian’, ‘entertain, provide for’ (a rare word, so the sense comes from the lexica), and ‘willum’ a dative plural of ‘willa’, ‘wish, desire’, so ‘supplied as we wished’. The comma after ‘tela’ is Klaeber’s, and the clause is a statement, not a question, though the verb comes first.

sentences.t: þū ūs wēl dohtest.
sentences.l: you for us well availed.
sentences.i: you have served us well.
sentences.n: ‘dohtest’ is the second person singular past of ‘dugan’, ‘avail, be of use, be good’, with ‘ūs’ a dative, ‘to us’; ‘þū ūs wēl dohtest’ is ‘you were of good use to us’, ‘you did us good’. ‘dugan’ is the root of ‘duguð’, the body of proven warriors met at 1790, so it carries the sense of worth shown in deeds. This sentence answers the courtesies of the previous clause: they have been hosted as they wished, and Hrothgar was the cause.

sentences.t:
Gif ic þonne on eorþan ōwihte mæg
þīnre mōdlufan māran tilian,
gumena dryhten, ðonne ic gȳt dyde,
gūðgeweorca, ic bēo gearo sōna.
sentences.l: If I then on earth in any whit can, of your mind-love, more win, lord of men, than I yet did, of war-deeds, I will be ready at once.
sentences.i: If I can in any way on earth win more of your heart’s love than I have yet done, lord of men, by deeds of war, I shall be ready at once.
sentences.n: A condition and its result: ‘Gif ic … mæg … tilian’ is ‘if I am able to strive for’ and ‘ic bēo gearo sōna’ ‘I will be ready at once’, ‘bēo’ the form of ‘bēon’ that looks forward (‘will be’). ‘tilian’ takes a genitive, ‘strive for, win’, and I take ‘māran’ as a noun, ‘more’ (accusative singular), with ‘þīnre mōdlufan’ a genitive after it, ‘more of your mind-love’ (‘mōdlufu’, ‘mind-love’; ‘þīnre’ is the feminine genitive); ‘i’ says ‘heart’s love’ for it. The other possibility is that ‘māran’ agrees with ‘mōdlufan’, ‘your greater mind-love’; the construction is hard, and this is my reading of it. ‘þonne’ after ‘Gif ic’ is ‘then, in that case’. ‘on eorþan ōwihte’ is ‘on earth in any whit’, that is, in any way at all. ‘gumena dryhten’ is a vocative, ‘lord of men’, Hrothgar. ‘ðonne ic gȳt dyde’ is ‘than I have yet done’, ‘ðonne’ meaning ‘than’; ‘gūðgeweorca’ is a genitive plural, ‘of war-deeds’, and I put it into English as ‘by deeds of war’; whether it is a partitive genitive after ‘māran’ or ‘dyde’, or depends on ‘tilian’ itself, is not settled by the grammar, and the choice is a guess.

sentences.t:
Gif ic þæt gefricge ofer flōda begang,
þæt þec ymbsittend egesan þȳwað,
swā þec hetende hwīlum dydon,
sentences.l: If I learn it, over the circuit of floods, that around-sitters threaten you with terror, as haters at times did to you,
sentences.i: If I hear, across the wide sea, that your neighbours threaten you with terror, as enemies have done to you at times,
sentences.n: The apparatus marks the start of a new manuscript leaf (fol. 170a) at ‘fricge’. ‘Gif ic þæt gefricge’ is ‘if I learn it’, the first ‘þæt’ pointing ahead to the clause in the next line, and ‘gefricge’ a present form (the same in the indicative and subjunctive) of ‘gefricgean’, ‘learn by asking, hear’. ‘ofer flōda begang’ is ‘over the circuit of floods’, which I take with ‘gefricge’ (‘hear across the sea’); ‘begang’ is ‘circuit, expanse’ as at 362, and ‘begong’ at 1497, and ‘flōda’ is a genitive plural: the sea between the Geats and the Danes. ‘ymbsittend’ is ‘neighbours’, literally ‘those sitting around’, the word of the prologue’s ‘ymbsittendra’ at 9 (‘around-sitters’ there), here the subject of ‘þȳwað’, ‘press, threaten’, with ‘egesan’ a dative (it could be an accusative), ‘with terror’. ‘swā þec hetende hwīlum dydon’ is ‘as haters sometimes did to you’: ‘hetende’ is a participle used as a noun, ‘those who hate’, and ‘dydon’ a plural past of ‘dōn’, with ‘þec’ the longer accusative of ‘you’. The apparatus lists ‘hettende’ for ‘hetende’ in several editors, and ‘dǣdon’, ‘dēdon’ and Sedgefield’s ‘ðȳdon’ for ‘dydon’; Klaeber prints ‘hetende’ and ‘dydon’.

sentences.t:
ic ðē þūsenda þegna bringe,
hæleþa tō helpe.
sentences.l: I will bring you thousands of thanes, of heroes, to help.
sentences.i: I will bring you thousands of thanes, warriors, to help you.
sentences.n: The result of the condition. ‘ic ðē … bringe’ is ‘I shall bring you’: ‘bringe’ is a present form used as a future, and ‘ðē’ is ‘to you’. ‘þūsenda’ is ‘thousands’, followed by a genitive plural, ‘þegna’ ‘of thanes’, and ‘hæleþa’ a second genitive plural, ‘of heroes’, in apposition, with ‘tō helpe’ ‘to help’. Both ‘l’ and ‘i’ keep the plural ‘thousands’ of the Old English. Beowulf is promising an army, and the next lines give the reason he can: his confidence in Higelac.

sentences.t:
Ic on Higelāce wāt,
Gēata dryhten, þēah ðe hē geong sŷ,
folces hyrde, þæt hē mec fremman wile
wordum ond weorcum,
sentences.l: I know of Higelac, lord of the Geats, though he be young, the people’s herdsman, that he will further me with words and with works,
sentences.i: I know of Higelac, lord of the Geats, though he is young, the shepherd of his people, that he will back me with words and with deeds,
sentences.n: ‘Ic on Higelāce wāt’ is ‘I know of Higelac’ (or ‘I rely on Higelac’): ‘witan on’ with a dative of the person is ‘know about, count on’, which is my reading of a short phrase. ‘Gēata dryhten’ and ‘folces hyrde’ (‘the people’s herdsman’, a stock phrase for a king, as at 610) stand beside the dative in apposition; ‘dryhten’ is nominative, so the case does not agree, and the apparatus says that Kluge and Sedgefield print the dative ‘dryhtne’ to mend that. ‘þēah ðe hē geong sŷ’ is ‘though he be young’, ‘sŷ’ a present subjunctive of ‘bēon’, ‘be’; the circumflex is Klaeber’s contraction mark. The apparatus adds that Trautmann and Holthausen print ‘Higelāc’ without ‘-e’, and cites Sedgefield for ‘Ic wāt on Higelāce’ without saying how his line differs; it also says the manuscript’s ‘wāt’ was altered from ‘wac’ in a different ink. ‘þæt hē mec fremman wile’ is ‘that he will further me’, ‘fremman’ ‘help on, carry out’, and ‘mec’ the longer accusative ‘me’. Klaeber’s italics in ‘wordum’ (o) and ‘weorcum’ (eo) mark an emendation: the manuscript has ‘weordum ond worcum’, and the apparatus says Thorkelin, Schücking and Chambers print ‘wordum ond weorcum’ as Klaeber does, while Heyne, Holthausen and Sedgefield print ‘wordum ond worcum’.

sentences.t:
þæt ic þē wēl herige
ond þē tō gēoce gārholt bere,
mægenes fultum, þǣr ðē bið manna þearf.
sentences.l: that I may well praise you and bear the spear-wood to your help, a support of strength, where there is need of men for you.
sentences.i: so that I may honour you well and bear a spear to your aid, a strong support, wherever you have need of men.
sentences.n: A second ‘þæt’ clause after ‘fremman wile’, giving the purpose of Higelac’s help: ‘þæt ic þē wēl herige’ is ‘that I may well praise you’, ‘herige’ a present form of ‘herian’, ‘praise, honour’, subjunctive in a purpose clause, so Higelac’s help is meant to let Beowulf honour Hrothgar in deed. ‘gārholt’ is ‘spear-wood’ (‘gār’ ‘spear’ and ‘holt’ ‘wood’, a spear-shaft; the whole word stands for the spear), the object of ‘bere’, ‘bear’, and ‘mægenes fultum’ is ‘support of strength’, in apposition, the whole help Beowulf brings. ‘tō gēoce’ is ‘to help’. ‘þǣr ðē bið manna þearf’ is ‘where there is need of men for you’: ‘þearf’ is a noun, ‘need’, with a genitive ‘manna’, and ‘ðē’ a dative.

sentences.l: If then Hrethric, a king’s child, resorts to him, to the courts of the Geats, he can find there many friends;
sentences.i: If Hrethric, a king’s son, should come to him at the court of the Geats, he can find many friends there;
sentences.n: ‘Gif … geþingeð’ is ‘if … resorts’: ‘geþingeð’ is a present form whose lemma I do not know for certain, and I take it from the context as ‘come, resort’, which is a guess (the manuscript has ‘geþinged’; the apparatus says Kemble prints ‘geþingað’ and Grein ‘geþingeð’, which Klaeber follows). ‘Hrēþrīc’ is Hrothgar’s son, named with his brother Hrothmund at 1189 (there spelled ‘Hrēðrīc’); ‘þēodnes bearn’ is ‘a king’s child’, ‘þēodnes’ a genitive. Klaeber’s italic ‘c’ marks a change: the manuscript has ‘hreþrinc’, and Grundtvig (‘Gru. tr.’) has ‘Hrēþrīc’, which is printed. ‘him’ is a dative that is either reflexive, ‘for himself’ (Hrethric), or names Higelac, ‘to him’, at whose court the visitor would arrive; the grammar does not say which, and I take the second. ‘tō hofum Gēata’ is ‘to the courts of the Geats’, ‘hofum’ a dative plural. ‘hē mæg þǣr fela frēonda findan’ is ‘he can find there many friends’, ‘fela’ taking the genitive ‘frēonda’. Beowulf is offering Hrothgar’s son a welcome at Higelac’s court. The semicolon sets the next clause against this one.

sentences.t:
feorcȳþðe bēoð
sēlran gesōhte þǣm þe him selfa dēah.’
sentences.l: far lands are better sought by one who is himself of worth.’
sentences.i: Far lands are better visited by a man of worth.’
sentences.n: ‘feorcȳþðe’ is ‘far lands’ (‘feorr’ ‘far’ and ‘cȳþþ’ ‘native land, region’), a nominative plural and the subject of ‘bēoð’, ‘are’, which here states a general truth. ‘sēlran gesōhte’ is ‘better sought’: ‘sēlran’ is a comparative adjective and ‘gesōhte’ a plural past participle of ‘gesēcan’, ‘seek out, visit’. ‘þǣm þe him selfa dēah’ is ‘by him who is himself of worth’: ‘þǣm’ is a dative, ‘dēah’ the third person singular of ‘dugan’ (the verb of ‘dohtest’ at 1821), and ‘him selfa’ a reflexive dative with a nominative ‘selfa’, a loose construction that means ‘who is himself good’. Beowulf is saying that a worthy man can travel and be welcome. Klaeber’s closing quotation mark ends this speech; Hrothgar’s own reply starts at 1841.

sentences.t: Hrōðgār maþelode him on andsware:
sentences.l: Hrothgar spoke in speech-words to him in answer:
sentences.i: Hrothgar spoke to him in formal words, in answer:
sentences.n: The house formula again, with ‘him on andsware’ added: ‘him’ is a dative, ‘to him’, and ‘on andsware’ ‘in answer’, ‘andsware’ a dative of ‘andswaru’. ‘Hrōðgār maþelode’ gives the king’s reply the same weight as Beowulf’s speech, and the colon says the speech follows at once.

sentences.t:
‘Þē þā wordcwydas wigtig Drihten
on sefan sende;
sentences.l: ‘These word-sayings the wise Lord sent to you, into your mind;
sentences.i: ‘The wise Lord sent these words into your mind;
sentences.n: ‘Þē … on sefan sende’ is ‘sent into your mind’, ‘þē’ a dative, ‘sefan’ a dative of ‘sefa’, ‘mind’. ‘sende’ is a past form that is the same in indicative and subjunctive, so the mood cannot be read from it; I render a plain ‘sent’, though Hrothgar may be inferring the cause of the words, which would add a shade of ‘must have’ that nothing in the form marks. ‘wordcwydas’ is ‘word-sayings, speeches’ (‘cwide’ ‘saying’), an accusative plural. ‘wigtig’ occurs only here in the poem and is a puzzle: I take it as a spelling of ‘wītig’, ‘wise’, as in ‘wītig Drihten’ at 1554, which suits a Lord who puts wisdom in a man’s mind, and the other possibility, from ‘wīg’ ‘war’, makes ‘Drihten’ a war-skilled God, which is less likely and is another guess. ‘Drihten’ is the Lord, God. The opening quotation mark is Klaeber’s.

sentences.t:
ne hȳrde ic snotorlīcor
on swā geongum feore guman þingian.
sentences.l: I have not heard a man speak more wisely in so young a life.
sentences.i: I have never heard a man of such youth speak more wisely.
sentences.n: ‘ne hȳrde ic’ is ‘I did not hear’, followed by an accusative and an infinitive, ‘guman þingian’, ‘a man speak’: ‘hȳran’ takes a bare infinitive after its object, and ‘guman’ is an accusative singular. ‘snotorlīcor’ is the comparative adverb of ‘snotorlīce’, ‘wisely’, and ‘þingian’ is ‘speak, plead’. ‘on swā geongum feore’ is ‘in so young a life’, ‘feore’ a dative of ‘feorh’, ‘life’. As in the prologue’s ‘ne hȳrde ic cȳmlīcor’ (38), the past tense with ‘ne’ means ‘I have never heard’. Hrothgar means that he has never heard such wisdom from so young a man.

sentences.t:
Þū eart mægenes strang, ond on mōde frōd,
wīs wordcwida!
sentences.l: You are strong in might, and old in mind, wise in speeches!
sentences.i: You are strong in might, ripe in mind, wise in what you say!
sentences.n: ‘Þū eart’ is ‘you are’, and ‘mægenes strang’ is ‘strong in might’, ‘mægenes’ a genitive of respect (‘with regard to might’). ‘frōd’ is ‘old, wise, experienced’, here applied to ‘mōde’, a dative, ‘in mind’, so the mind of a young man is old; ‘frōd’ is the root of ‘infrōdum’ at 1874. ‘wīs wordcwida’ is ‘wise of speeches’, ‘wordcwida’ a genitive plural, again a respect: wise in what is said. Klaeber’s exclamation mark is his punctuation, and the three phrases are a list of praise with no verb after the first.

sentences.t:
Wēn ic talige,
gif þæt gegangeð, þæt ðe gār nymeð,
hild heorugrimme Hrēþles eaferan,
ādl oþðe īren ealdor ðīnne,
folces hyrde, ond þū þīn feorh hafast,
sentences.l: Expectation I reckon, if it come about that spear, battle sword-grim, sickness or iron takes Hrethel’s offspring, your chief, the people’s herdsman, and you have your life,
sentences.i: I think it likely that, if it should happen that spear or fierce battle, sickness or iron takes the son of Hrethel, your chief, the shepherd of the people, and you still have your life,
sentences.n: ‘Wēn ic talige’ is ‘I count it an expectation’: ‘wēn’ is ‘hope, expectation’ and need not be happy (the published parts’ ‘hope’ is the same word); ‘talige’ is a present of ‘talian’, ‘reckon’, and ‘i’ puts the pair as ‘I think it likely’. The ‘gif’ clause is ‘gif þæt gegangeð, þæt …’, ‘if it comes about, that …’ (‘þæt ðe’ I take as ‘that’ with the particle ‘ðe’, not the pronoun ‘from you’), and its subjects, joined without conjunctions at first, are ‘gār’ ‘spear’, ‘hild heorugrimme’ ‘sword-grim battle’ (‘heoro-’ as at 1780, where its force is doubtful), ‘ādl’ ‘sickness’ and ‘īren’ ‘iron’, one singular ‘nymeð’ (‘takes’) for all. The object is ‘Hrēþles eaferan’, ‘Hrethel’s offspring’, a singular (‘eaferan’ is the accusative singular of the weak ‘eafera’), who is Higelac, Hrethel’s son, and ‘ealdor ðīnne’ (‘your chief’, an accusative) and ‘folces hyrde’ (‘shepherd of the people’) are in apposition to him. ‘ond þū þīn feorh hafast’ is ‘and you have your life’, still alive. What Hrothgar expects to follow is said in the next unit.

sentences.t:
þæt þe Sǣ-Gēatas sēlran næbben
tō gecēosenne cyning ǣnigne,
hordweard hæleþa, gyf þū healdan wylt
māga rīce.
sentences.l: that the Sea-Geats have not a better one to choose, any king, hoard-guard of heroes, if you will hold the kinsmen’s realm.
sentences.i: then the Geats will have no better man to choose as king, the heroes’ hoard-keeper, if you are willing to hold the kingdom of your kinsmen.
sentences.n: ‘þæt þe Sǣ-Gēatas sēlran næbben’ is ‘that the Sea-Geats have not a better’: ‘næbben’ is ‘ne habben’, a subjunctive after the ‘wēn’ clause, and ‘þæt þe’ is ‘that’ with the particle ‘þe’ (it could be read as the pronoun ‘þē’, ‘for you’, but the sense does not need it); ‘sēlran’ is a comparative used as a noun, ‘a better one’, ‘ǣnigne’ the accusative of ‘any’ going with ‘cyning’, and ‘tō gecēosenne’ an inflected infinitive, ‘to choose’. ‘Sǣ-Gēatas’ is ‘Sea-Geats’, the Geats named by the sea they live beside (the same people as the Weder-Geats, ‘storm-Geats’, of other lines). The apparatus marks the start of a new manuscript leaf (fol. 170b) at ‘sǣ’. ‘hordweard hæleþa’ is ‘hoard-guard of heroes’, in apposition to ‘cyning’ (‘hordweard’, ‘treasure-keeper’, is a poetic word for a king, used of Hrothgar at 1047 in the same phrase). ‘gyf þū healdan wylt māga rīce’ is ‘if you will hold the kinsmen’s realm’ (the Geats are Beowulf’s kin), ‘māga’ a genitive plural of ‘māg’, ‘kinsman’, and ‘rīce’ ‘realm’. Hrothgar means that the Geats could not choose a better king than Beowulf. I read ‘hordweard’ as describing the king in general, and I cannot rule out that it is aimed at Beowulf himself.

sentences.t:
Mē þīn mōdsefa
līcað leng swā wēl, lēofa Bēowulf.
sentences.l: Your mind pleases me the longer the better, dear Beowulf.
sentences.i: Your mind pleases me more and more as time goes on, dear Beowulf.
sentences.n: ‘Mē … līcað’ is ‘pleases me’, ‘līcian’ taking a dative of the person pleased, with ‘þīn mōdsefa’ (‘your mind-spirit’, ‘mōd’ ‘mind’ and ‘sefa’ ‘mind’) as subject. ‘leng swā wēl’ is ‘the longer, the better’, ‘leng’ ‘longer’ and ‘swā wēl’ ‘so well’, an idiom in which the second term grows as the first does; the apparatus records Grein’s Sprachschatz, Holthausen, Schücking and Sedgefield printing ‘sēl’ in place of ‘wēl’, ‘E.’ (Earle, I take it, as in the earlier parts) ‘bet’, and Bugge ‘bet’ or ‘sēl’, all ‘better’; Klaeber keeps ‘wēl’. ‘lēofa Bēowulf’ is the vocative with the weak adjective, as at 1758.

sentences.t:
Hafast þū gefēred, þæt þām folcum sceal,
Gēata lēodum ond Gār-Denum
sib gemǣne, ond sacu restan,
inwitnīþas, þē hīe ǣr drugon,
wesan, þenden ic wealde wīdan rīces,
sentences.l: You have brought it about that, for the peoples, for the Geat-folk and the Spear-Danes, peace in common shall be, and strife rest, the malicious hatreds that they formerly practised, while I rule the wide realm,
sentences.i: You have accomplished this: that the two peoples, the Geats and the Spear-Danes, shall have peace in common, and strife shall rest, the wicked hatreds that they practised before, for as long as I rule my wide kingdom,
sentences.n: ‘Hafast þū gefēred’ is ‘you have brought about’ (‘gefēran’, ‘carry out, bring to pass’), and the ‘þæt’ clause says what: ‘þæt þām folcum sceal … sib gemǣne … wesan’, ‘that for the peoples peace shall be in common’, with ‘sceal’ and ‘wesan’ framing the clause and ‘sib’ ‘peace, kinship’. ‘sacu restan’ is ‘strife shall rest’ (‘sacu’ ‘strife’, a nominative singular, with ‘restan’ an infinitive after ‘sceal’), and ‘inwitnīþas, þē hīe ǣr drugon’ is ‘the malicious hatreds that they formerly practised’: ‘inwitnīþ’ is ‘hostile malice’ (‘inwit’ ‘malice, guile’ and ‘nīð’ ‘hatred’), a plural here and the object of ‘drugon’, the plural past of ‘drēogan’, ‘carry out’; ‘þē’ is the relative particle. Klaeber’s italic final ‘e’ in ‘gemǣne’ marks his change: the manuscript has ‘ge mænum’, which would be a dative plural, ‘for the peoples in common’, and Sievers’s ‘gemǣne’ (‘common’) is printed. ‘þenden ic wealde wīdan rīces’ is ‘while I rule the wide realm’, ‘wealdan’ taking a genitive, ‘rīces’; ‘þenden’ is ‘while’. ‘Gār-Denum’ is a dative plural of ‘Gār-Dene’, ‘Spear-Danes’, and ‘Gēata lēodum’ ‘the people of the Geats’. The comma after ‘rīces’ leads on to the second pledge, treasures.

sentences.t:
māþmas gemǣne, manig ōþerne
gōdum gegrēttan ofer ganotes bæð;
sentences.l: treasures in common, many a man another with good things shall greet over the gannet’s bath;
sentences.i: and treasures shall be shared, and many a man shall greet another with gifts across the sea;
sentences.n: ‘māþmas gemǣne’ is ‘treasures in common’, a nominative plural, with ‘wesan’ understood from the last unit. ‘manig ōþerne gōdum gegrēttan’ is ‘many (a man) to greet another with good things’, ‘manig’ a singular used for ‘many a one’, ‘gegrēttan’ an infinitive (‘greet, approach’) after the ‘sceal’ of the last unit, and ‘gōdum’ a dative plural used as a noun, ‘with good things’, meaning gifts. ‘ganotes bæð’ is ‘the gannet’s bath’, a kenning for the sea, first met in this part: the ‘ganot’ is the gannet, a sea-bird that dives, so its bath is the open water. The semicolon closes the promise about exchange of gifts and a second clause says how they are to travel.

sentences.t:
sceal hringnaca ofer heafu bringan
lāc ond luftācen.
sentences.l: shall the ring-boat bring gifts over the seas, and love-tokens.
sentences.i: a ship with ringed prow shall carry gifts over the seas, and tokens of love.
sentences.n: ‘sceal … bringan’ is ‘shall bring’, with ‘hringnaca’ (‘ring-boat’: ‘hring’ ‘ring’ and ‘naca’ ‘boat’) as subject, a poetic word for a ship, whose ‘ring’ may be the coiled or banded prow or the rings of its fastenings; the exact picture is a guess. ‘ofer heafu’ is ‘over the seas’, ‘heafu’ an accusative plural of ‘heaf’, ‘sea’. Klaeber’s italic ‘f’ marks his change: the manuscript has ‘hea þu’, as two words, and Klaeber, with Kluge, Sievers and four editors, prints ‘heafu’. The apparatus also says that an ‘l’ after ‘sceal’ was erased in the manuscript. ‘lāc’ is ‘gift’, and ‘luftācen’ is ‘love-token’ (‘lufu’ ‘love’ and ‘tācen’ ‘token’), a word the poem has nowhere else, so the compound rests on its parts. Hrothgar is picturing gifts crossing the sea in both directions.

sentences.t:
Ic þā lēode wāt
gē wið fēond gē wið frēond fæste geworhte,
ǣghwæs untǣle ealde wīsan.’
sentences.l: I know the peoples, both toward foe and toward friend, firmly made, blameless in everything, in the old way.’
sentences.i: I know that these two peoples are steadfast both toward foe and toward friend, blameless in every respect, in the old way.’
sentences.n: ‘Ic þā lēode wāt … fæste geworhte’ is ‘I know the people firmly wrought’: ‘wāt’ takes an accusative and a participle, ‘geworhte’ the plural past participle of ‘gewyrcan’, ‘make’, so the peoples are as if built firm, loyal. ‘gē wið fēond gē wið frēond’ is ‘both toward foe and toward friend’, the pair ‘gē … gē’ ‘both … and’, with ‘wið’ and the accusative. ‘ǣghwæs untǣle’ is ‘blameless in everything’, ‘ǣghwæs’ a genitive of respect and ‘untǣle’ ‘free from blame’ (‘tǣl’ ‘blame’), and ‘ealde wīsan’ is an accusative of manner, ‘in the old fashion’, ‘wīse’ ‘way, manner’. The mark ’ at the end is Klaeber’s closing quotation mark for Hrothgar’s speech, which began at 1841. ‘Ic þā lēode wāt’ means that Hrothgar, like Beowulf at 1830, claims to know the people he speaks of.

sentences.t:
Ðā gīt him eorla hlēo inne gesealde,
mago Healfdenes māþmas twelfe;
sentences.l: Then yet gave him, within, the shelter of earls, son of Healfdene, twelve treasures;
sentences.i: Then the protector of earls, Healfdene’s son, gave him in the hall twelve treasures besides;
sentences.n: ‘Ðā gīt’ is ‘then still’, that is ‘then further’, introducing one more act. ‘eorla hlēo’ is the ‘shelter of earls’ said of Beowulf at 791 and of Hrothgar at 1035, here again Hrothgar, and ‘mago Healfdenes’ is ‘son of Healfdene’, ‘mago’ a nominative of ‘magu’, ‘son, kinsman, young man’; both are in apposition to the unnamed subject of ‘gesealde’, ‘gave’. ‘inne’ is ‘within’, ‘him’ a dative, and ‘māþmas twelfe’ ‘twelve treasures’. The manuscript has the numeral ‘.xii.’, and Klaeber writes the word out as ‘twelfe’, as the apparatus says. The semicolon after ‘twelfe’ gives way to the king’s last order.

sentences.t:
hēt [h]ine mid þǣm lācum lēode swǣse
sēcean on gesyntum, snūde eft cuman.
sentences.l: He bade him, with those gifts, seek his dear people in safety, and quickly come again.
sentences.i: He bade him go with those gifts to his own dear people, in safety, and come back quickly.
sentences.n: ‘hēt’ is ‘bade’, with an accusative and two infinitives: ‘[h]ine … sēcean’ ‘him seek’ and ‘cuman’ ‘come’. The manuscript has ‘inne’, which the apparatus says Thorkelin changed to ‘hine’; Klaeber prints ‘[h]ine’ with the ‘h’ in brackets as added, and the ‘e’ is also in italics, a sign of change whose reason the apparatus does not give. ‘mid þǣm lācum’ is ‘with those gifts’, ‘lācum’ a dative plural. ‘lēode swǣse’ is ‘his dear people’, ‘swǣs’ ‘dear, own’, an accusative plural. ‘on gesyntum’ is ‘in good health, safely’ (‘gesynto’ ‘health, safety’, dative plural), and ‘snūde eft cuman’ is ‘quickly come back’. Hrothgar is bidding him come back, which prepares for the farewell that follows.

sentences.l: Then the king, good in noble qualities, the prince of the Scyldings, kissed the best of thanes and took him by the neck;
sentences.i: Then the king, a man of noble worth, lord of the Scyldings, kissed the best of thanes and put his arms about his neck;
sentences.n: ‘Gecyste’ is ‘kissed’, the past of ‘gecyssan’, with ‘þā’ ‘then’; the verb comes first, its subject is ‘cyning æþelum gōd’, ‘king good in noble qualities’ (‘æþelum’ a dative plural of respect) with ‘þēoden Scyldinga’, ‘prince of the Scyldings’, in apposition, and its object is Beowulf, ‘ðegn[a] betstan’. ‘l’ puts the subject first so that the English does not read as if the prince of the Scyldings were the one kissed. ‘ðegn[a] betstan’ is ‘the best of thanes’: ‘betstan’ is a weak accusative singular, the object of ‘gecyste’, and ‘ðegn[a]’ the genitive plural ‘of thanes’, the final ‘a’ in brackets because Klaeber added it. The manuscript has ‘ðegn’, and the apparatus says that Kemble, Schubert, Sievers and four more make the same change (it refers to the notes on 947a and 1759a, and compare ‘secg[a] betsta’ at 1759). ‘be healse genam’ is ‘took by the neck’, an embrace (‘heals’ ‘neck’ is the first part of ‘healsgebedda’ at 63).

sentences.t:
hruron him tēaras
blondenfeaxum.
sentences.l: Tears fell from him, from the blended-haired one.
sentences.i: Tears fell from the grey-haired king.
sentences.n: ‘hruron’ is the plural past of ‘hrēosan’, ‘fall’, with ‘tēaras’ as subject and ‘him blondenfeaxum’ a dative, ‘to/from him, the blended-haired’; the sense is that the tears ran from the old king. ‘blondenfeax’ is the word of 1791, there taken as hair mixed with grey. Hrothgar weeps openly at parting, and the next unit says why.

sentences.t:
Him wæs bēga wēn
ealdum infrōdum, ōþres swīðor,
þæt h[ī]e seoðða(n) [nō] gesēon mōston,
mōdige on meþle.
sentences.l: To them was expectation of both, to the old, very wise one, of the other more, that they afterwards might not see each other, high-spirited, in meeting.
sentences.i: Both of them expected it, but the old and very wise king more than the other: that they might never see each other again, those high-spirited men, in council.
sentences.n: ‘Him wæs bēga wēn’ is ‘to them was expectation of both’: ‘him’ is a dative, ‘bēga’ a genitive plural of ‘bēgen’, ‘both’, and ‘wēn’ is ‘expectation’, the word at 1845. ‘ealdum infrōdum’ is ‘to the old, very wise one’, datives that I take to mean Hrothgar alone, and ‘ōþres swīðor’ is literally ‘of the other more’, ‘ōþres’ a genitive and ‘swīðor’ the comparative adverb ‘more’. Old English would put ‘than’ before a comparison, so ‘more than the other’ in ‘i’ is my reading and not what the grammar states; the phrase could also mean that the expectation concerned the other man more, and that is a guess. The apparatus marks the start of a new manuscript leaf (fol. 171a) at ‘frodum’. The ‘þæt’ clause is the thing expected: ‘þæt h[ī]e seoðða(n) [nō] gesēon mōston’ is ‘that they might not see each other afterwards’. Three small restorations are in the line. The manuscript has ‘he’ and Grundtvig (‘Gru. tr.’) ‘hīe’, so Klaeber puts ‘ī’ in brackets (‘they’); the final ‘n’ of ‘seoðða(n)’ is in parentheses, restored where the manuscript is lost; and the negative ‘[nō]’ is added by Klaeber (‘nā’ in Bugge, Sievers, Holthausen, Sedgefield and Chambers, with the same meaning), because without it the clause would say that they expected to meet again, which is not what the context needs. ‘mōdige’ is a nominative plural, ‘high-spirited, brave’, and ‘on meþle’ ‘in meeting’, ‘meþel’ meaning an assembly or conference, the place where such men speak.

sentences.t:
Wæs him se man tō þon lēof,
þæt hē þone brēostwylm forberan ne mehte;
sentences.l: The man was so dear to him that he could not hold back the breast-welling;
sentences.i: The man was so dear to him that he could not hold back the welling of feeling in his breast;
sentences.n: ‘Wæs him se man tō þon lēof, þæt …’ is ‘the man was so dear to him that …’: ‘tō þon … þæt’ is ‘so … that’, ‘him’ a dative, and ‘se man’ Beowulf. ‘þone brēostwylm’ is ‘the breast-welling’ (‘brēost’ ‘breast’ and ‘wylm’ ‘surge, boiling’, as in ‘flōdes wylm’ at 1764), the rush of feeling, and ‘forberan ne mehte’ is ‘could not forbear, hold back’. Hrothgar’s tears at 1872 are that welling.

sentences.t:
ac him on hreþre hygebendum fæst
æfter dēorum men dyrne langað
born wið blōde.
sentences.l: but in his breast, fast in mind-bonds, a hidden longing for the dear man burned against the blood.
sentences.i: but fast in the bonds of his mind, within his breast, a hidden longing for the dear man burned against his blood.
sentences.n: This line is uncertain, and I give my reading as a guess. ‘him on hreþre hygebendum fæst’ is ‘in his breast, fast in mind-bonds’: ‘hreþre’ is a dative of ‘hreþer’, ‘breast’, and ‘hygebendum’ (‘hyge’ ‘mind’ and ‘bend’ ‘bond’) a dative plural, ‘with mind-bonds’, the longing being bound inside him. ‘æfter dēorum men’ is ‘for the dear man’, ‘æfter’ ‘after, for’ with a dative. ‘dyrne langað’ is ‘hidden longing’, ‘dyrne’ ‘hidden, secret’; ‘langað’ may be a noun (‘longing’) or a present verb (‘longs’), and Klaeber’s ‘born’ (italic ‘o’) forces the noun, because ‘born’ is the past of ‘beornan’, ‘burn’, and ‘a longing burned’ is the clause. The manuscript has ‘beorn’, ‘warrior’, which makes ‘langað’ a verb and Hrothgar the subject (‘a man longs … against the blood’); the apparatus says that Thorkelin, Sievers and three more editors read ‘born’, and Grein, Wyatt and Chambers ‘bearn’, ‘child’. ‘wið blōde’ is ‘against the blood’ (‘wið’ with a dative), and ‘i’ keeps ‘against his blood’. Whether the longing presses on the blood in his body, or fights what the bond of kinship would ask, or ‘wið’ stands loosely for ‘in’, I cannot tell from the grammar; that is a guess.

sentences.l: From him Beowulf, war-man, gold-proud, trod the grass-ground, exultant in treasure;
sentences.i: Then Beowulf went away from him, a warrior proud in gold, over the grassy earth, jubilant with treasure;
sentences.n: ‘Him … þanan’ is ‘from him, thence’, ‘him’ a dative and ‘þanan’ ‘from there’; ‘Bēowulf’ is the subject of ‘træd’, ‘trod’, the past of ‘tredan’. ‘gūðrinc’ is ‘war-man’ (‘gūð’ ‘battle’ and ‘rinc’ ‘man, warrior’), ‘goldwlanc’ ‘gold-proud’ (‘wlanc’ ‘proud, splendid’), and ‘græsmoldan’ is ‘grass-ground’ (‘græs’ ‘grass’ and ‘molde’ ‘earth’), an accusative. ‘since hrēmig’ is ‘exultant in treasure’, ‘hrēmig’ ‘exulting’ with a dative of the cause, ‘since’, ‘treasure’. The twelve treasures given at 1867 are what he is exultant over. The semicolon closes the walk and the next unit turns to the ship.

sentences.t:
sǣgenga bād
āge[n]dfreân, sē þe on ancre rād.
sentences.l: The sea-goer awaited its owner-lord, that at anchor rode.
sentences.i: The ship that rode at anchor waited for its lord.
sentences.n: ‘sǣgenga’ is ‘sea-goer’ (‘sǣ’ ‘sea’ and ‘genga’ ‘goer’), a poetic word for the ship, the subject of ‘bād’, ‘awaited’ (the past of ‘bīdan’, which takes a genitive or an accusative). ‘āge[n]dfreân’ is ‘its owner-lord’ (‘āgend’ ‘owner’ and ‘frea’ ‘lord’), here Beowulf as the ship’s master; the manuscript has ‘aged-frean’ and Kemble supplied the ‘n’, which Klaeber puts in brackets. The circumflex in ‘freân’ is hard to read in the page image: its apex sits in the gap between ‘e’ and ‘a’, slightly toward ‘e’, and I take it as the contraction mark and place it on the second vowel, ‘freâ’, by the house rule; the reading is low-confidence. ‘sē þe on ancre rād’ is ‘which rode at anchor’, ‘sē’ a masculine relative for the ship, ‘ancre’ a dative of ‘ancor’, ‘anchor’ (a Latin loan), and ‘rād’ the past of ‘rīdan’, ‘ride’, said of a ship riding on the water.

sentences.t:
Þā wæs on gange gifu Hrōðgāres
oft geæhted;
sentences.l: Then was, on the way, Hrothgar’s gift often valued;
sentences.i: Then, as they went, Hrothgar’s gift was often praised;
sentences.n: ‘Þā wæs … oft geæhted’ is ‘then was often esteemed’, a passive with ‘gifu Hrōðgāres’, ‘Hrothgar’s gift’, as subject, ‘Hrōðgāres’ a genitive. ‘geæhted’ is the past participle of ‘geæhtan’, which I take as ‘value, esteem’ and render ‘praised’; the sense is from the lexica and is not certain, and who did the praising is not said. ‘on gange’ is ‘on the way, in going’, ‘gange’ a dative of ‘gang’, ‘going’; ‘as they went’ in ‘i’ is my reading, and ‘on gange’ might also mean ‘in progress, going about’, so that the gift is much talked of. The semicolon ends the account of the leave-taking and the poet turns to praise the giver.

sentences.t:
þæt wæs ān cyning
ǣghwæs orleahtre, oþ þæt hine yldo benam
mægenes wynnum, sē þe oft manegum scōd.
sentences.l: that was a unique king, blameless in everything, until old age took from him the joys of might, which has often harmed many.
sentences.i: That was a king without equal, blameless in every way, until old age took from him the joys of his strength, old age that has so often harmed men.
sentences.n: ‘þæt wæs ān cyning’ is ‘that was a unique king’, ‘ān’ ‘one, sole’ (‘a king indeed’ is the weaker alternative), and ‘ǣghwæs orleahtre’ is ‘blameless in every way’: ‘orleahtre’ is ‘without fault’ (‘or-’ ‘without’ and ‘leahtor’ ‘fault’), and ‘ǣghwæs’ a genitive of respect, as at 1865. ‘oþ þæt hine yldo benam’ is ‘until old age took from him’, ‘hine’ the accusative of the person (Hrothgar) and ‘mægenes wynnum’ a dative plural, ‘from the joys of strength’, since ‘beniman’ takes a dative of the thing taken. ‘sē þe oft manegum scōd’ is ‘who often harmed many’, ‘scōd’ the past of ‘sceððan’, ‘harm’, with a dative. The antecedent is a problem: ‘yldo’ is feminine, and the apparatus says Grein and others read ‘sēo’ (‘which’), which would agree; Klaeber keeps ‘sē’, masculine. I follow the sense, ‘old age, which has often harmed many’, and that is a guess; ‘sē’ could also refer to the king, but that does not suit ‘orleahtre’. The poet is making Hrothgar’s decline the cost of long life.
